title: A Prom for the Scholarship
premise: Paloma Sterling, a scholarship senior and anonymous whistleblower behind the account @SterlingTruth, has spent twelve years hiding his past after his father's wrongful conviction. When Ashford Prep's college essay prompt — 'What truth have you paid for?' — goes viral and classmates start confessing online, Paloma's account is doxxed by headmaster Whitlock's son, exposing the corruption in the school's scholarship fund. To keep his enrollment and clear his father's name, Paloma must win the state coding championship that secures his future while leading a student movement to expose the fund's theft before prom night, when Whitlock plans to announce the 'reformed' endowment. At prom itself, Paloma trades his championship prize money for the ledger that convicts Whitlock, wins both the title that matters and the girl who saw him first, and learns justice sometimes has to be built by hand.
about_author: Silas Okafor is a former debate coach who spent six years teaching at elite private schools before writing full-time. He lives in Lagos and Providence, splitting his year between them, and writes stories about kids who are too smart for the rooms they're allowed into.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Careful
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. We meet him mid-ritual: checking his burner, scrubbing metadata, rehearsing his 'narrative' for scholarship interviews. His mother works doubles; his father is twelve years into a sentence for a crime tied to Ashford's founding family. Emotional beat: the exhausting cost of invisibility, and the one crack in it — his anonymous account, @SterlingTruth, which knows too much about Ashford Prep.

chapters.title: The Question Nobody Can Stop Answering
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Senior English teacher Ms. Adeyemi assigns the Common App prompt 'What truth have you paid for?' and forbids sharing answers — which guarantees everyone shares them. Confessions flood a school forum. Paloma writes one he never posts. Beat: vertigo of honesty; the room feels dangerous and alive for the first time.

chapters.title: Juniper Reads the Room
chapters.summary: Juniper Vale's POV. The headmaster's daughter, brilliant and bored, reads the confessions like forensic evidence and starts mapping who's lying. She notices one confession was never posted but its phrasing matches @SterlingTruth's style exactly. Beat: her loneliness sharpening into obsession; she wants the truth-teller found, though she hasn't decided what for.

chapters.title: The Scholarship That Isn't
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma discovers the Sterling Scholarship — endowed for families wrongfully convicted by Ashford donors' testimony — has been quietly redirected for years, its money flowing to Whitlock's pet projects. The account posts the first thread. Beat: righteous fury curdling into fear as he realizes he's investigating the people who decide if he graduates.

chapters.title: Doxxed
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Whitlock's son Theo, humiliated by a thread, traces @SterlingTruth through a careless login from the library and posts the name. By morning the whole school knows. Juniper deletes it in ninety seconds — too late. Beat: twelve years of careful shattering in one screenshot; Paloma walks the halls feeling skinned.

chapters.title: The Offer You Can't Refuse Politely
chapters.summary: Whitlock's POV (first time inside the antagonist). Whitlock offers Paloma a deal: retract everything, take a quiet full ride to a lesser school, and his father's appeal 'might find friendly eyes.' He frames it as mercy. Beat: the seductive logic of power; Paloma says yes out loud and no inside.

chapters.title: State Championship Doesn't Matter
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The coding team — misfit crew including Theo, who codes beautifully and hates his father — qualifies for states. Coach tells them nobody outside the school cares. Paloma realizes the championship is cover: winners get press, press gets microphones. Beat: grim strategy replacing despair; the unimportant thing becomes the plan.

chapters.title: Juniper's Ledger
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper reveals she's been keeping her own records since she was fourteen — her father's passwords, board minutes, a pattern of 'donor adjustments.' She doesn't offer it out of goodness; she offers it because being complicit finally disgusts more than being loyal comforts. Beat: uneasy alliance, two liars recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Prom Is a Weapon
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Whitlock announces he'll unveil the 'restored' Sterling Scholarship at prom, with cameras. Paloma understands: it's a burial, not a restoration — a press release to kill the story forever. Prom becomes the deadline. Beat: dread converting to purpose; the most trivial night of senior year becomes the battlefield.

chapters.title: The Team That Hates Each Other
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. States prep implodes: Theo learns Paloma is the account that torched his family name; teammate Bex threatens to quit over Paloma's secrets hogging the spotlight. A brutal practice session ends in honesty — everyone confesses what they're actually competing for. Beat: fracture and reluctant glue; the team becomes real by breaking.

chapters.title: Visiting Day
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma visits his father, who begs him to stop — 'I survived by being small; don't you dare be loud for me.' Paloma shows him the ledger evidence instead. His father reads it twice, then teaches him something unexpected: how testimony actually works, where the weak points in a case live. Beat: inheritance reversed; the son arms the father.

chapters.title: Theo's Choice
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Whitlock asks Theo to plant a cheating accusation against Paloma before states. Theo sits with the code, his father's voice, and the memory of every dinner where silence was the price of love. He deletes the draft email — and copies himself on the fund's internal transfers instead. Beat: betrayal of blood for principle; terror and relief in the same breath.

chapters.title: States, Round One
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The competition opens; Ashford advances despite sabotage of their submission window — someone inside the league is helping Whitlock. Paloma codes through panic, and the team covers each other's gaps without being asked. Beat: flow state as refuge; competence as dignity when everything else is stripped away.

chapters.title: The Leak That Wasn't Mine
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Someone leaks half the ledger — doctored — making Paloma look like an extortionist. Juniper recognizes her own formatting habits in the forgery: someone used her files. She realizes her father knew about her all along. Beat: betrayal at the deepest level; her archive, her identity, weaponized against the boy she's starting to trust.

chapters.title: What Truth Have You Paid For
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Suspended pending investigation, Paloma finally submits his college essay — the whole story, names included, no anonymity left. Sending it feels like setting down a weight he'd mistaken for his spine. Beat: the essay prompt fulfilled; honesty chosen deliberately rather than forced, and it costs everything and frees him.

chapters.title: The Championship That Does Matter
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. States finals: Ashford versus the academy whose judge is compromised. The team builds redundancy into their entry so no single ruling can kill it, and wins cleanly, publicly, on stream. In the interview afterward, Paloma says his father's name and case number on camera. Beat: triumph used as a megaphone; the unimportant trophy becoming the loudest thing in the state.

chapters.title: Countdown to Prom
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Three days out: Whitlock accelerates the announcement, lawyers circle, Juniper's father gives her an ultimatum at breakfast. She copies the true ledger onto three drives and mails one to herself. Paloma and Juniper plan the prom intervention in the empty gym, slow-dancing once, absurdly, while mapping exits. Beat: tenderness under time pressure; love arriving sideways during a war.

chapters.title: Prom Night: The Unveiling
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Whitlock takes the stage amid fairy lights and cameras, unveiling the 'restored' scholarship with Paloma's face on the screen as its grateful beneficiary. Paloma walks up under the lights — invited, seemingly, to accept. Beat: the trap closing beautifully; the room holding its breath between applause and understanding.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. On stage, Paloma declines the check and plays the real ledger to the ballroom screens while Theo confirms the transfers live and Juniper's mailed drive lands with a journalist mid-speech. No police yet, no court — just two hundred witnesses who can't unknow it. Whitlock's composure cracks on camera. Beat: the climax; power exposed not by law but by community, witness by witness.

chapters.title: Aftermath in Fairy Lights
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The party continues around the wreckage — students dancing anyway, furious and giddy. Juniper and her father have their reckoning in the coat room; she chooses the drive over the family name. Paloma finds her and they finish the dance properly. Beat: grief and joy braided; the first honest celebration of their lives.

chapters.title: The Appeal
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Weeks later: the fund is frozen, Whitlock resigns under investigation, and Paloma's father's case reopens with new counsel and Theo's testimony. Paloma gets into the college of his choice — reading his essay aloud in admissions, apparently, all the way to the end. Beat: quiet vindication; the system moving, slowly, because people pushed it.

chapters.title: A Prom for the Scholarship
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue. The following spring, Ashford holds a rescheduled prom funded by the restored, genuinely restored scholarship — and Paloma's father, free on appeal, stands in the gym doorway in a rented suit. Paloma posts one last time as @SterlingTruth: 'Account closed. Tell the truth somewhere with your name on it.' Beat: belonging earned, not granted; the careful boy learning to be seen.
